background.definition: Mpox is caused by a dsDNA virus in the genus Orthopoxvirus in the family Poxviridae. In the 2022 outbreak, it caused rash (often peri-anal and peri-inguinal), fever, chills, myalgias, fatigue, headache, and respiratory symptoms. It is rarely fatal.

list.listitem: Ordinarily a rare infection, mpox is responsible for an outbreak that as of March 8, 2024 had affected 94,766 persons with 182 deaths in 117 countries. In the US, 42 deaths have been reported to date.(https://www.cdc.gov/poxvirus/monkeypox/response/2022/index.html)
Previously the disease was largely confined to countries in central and western Africa including the Congo, Gabon, the Central African Republic, Benin, and Sierra Leone.
From 2022 to 2024, 45,652 cases of mpox were reported to the Africa CDC with a case fatality rate of 3.3%.
During the first 13 weeks of 2024 664 mpox cases were reported in the US, primarily in New York (142), California (67) and Texas (43).
Mpox is caused by a dsDNA virus in the genus Orthopoxvirus in the family Poxviridae.

Tree squirrels, Gambian pouched rats, other rodents, and non-human primates have been cited as potential reservoirs of the virus. (https://www.cdc.gov/poxvirus/monkeypox/veterinarian/monkeypox-in-animals.html)
Zoonotic transmission can occur with contact to the blood, bodily fluids, or cutaneous lesions of infected animals.
In humans, it is spread by close physical contact, contact with respiratory secretions, or contact with a fomite (a contaminated object). Vertical transmission across the placenta may also occur.
A study of 528 infections in 16 countries found that 98% of persons were gay or bisexual, and for 95% sexual activity was the likely mechanism for transmission.
The strain circulating in the 2022 global outbreak was from clade 3 that initially caused an outbreak in Nigeria which causes less severe disease than clade 1.
The incubation period is typically 3 to 17 days. (https://www.cdc.gov/poxvirus/monkeypox/clinicians/clinical-recognition.html)

Risk_Factor.Risk_Name: Men who have sex with men

list.listitem: Two vaccines are available. Jynneos is a live, replication incompetent vaccinia virus vaccine given as 2 doses 4 weeks apart. It is preferred over ACAM2000® which is a live, replication competent vaccinia virus originally developed for smallpox. B

Preliminary data from CDC conclude that full vaccination with 2 doses of the Jynneos vaccine is 69% effective in preventing medically attended mpox disease, and 37% effective if only a single dose is received. This was confirmed in a published case-control study that found 66% effectiveness (95% CI 47% to 78%) for the JYNNEOS vaccine.
Effectiveness was confirmed in a test-negative case-control study in Canada that found 30% to 65% effectiveness depending on risk factor adjustment.
An FDA emergency use authorization allows administration of Jynneos intradermally at one-fifth the normal dose due to a shortage of vaccine in August, 2022. C

Vaccination is recommended by the CDC for close contacts of someone diagnosed with mpox and those at high risk for mpox. The latter includes people with multiple sexual partners or practicing group sex, sex at a sex club or bathhouse, or sex anywhere where mpox transmission is occurring. B
For persons with contraindications to vaccination, vaccinia immune globulin given IV is an option. (https://www.cdc.gov/poxvirus/monkeypox/clinicians/treatment.html)

Suspect mpox in a patient with characteristic rash, fever, and flu-like symptoms when the disease is circulating in a population. In the most recent outbreak (2022), it was most likely in men who have sex with men. C

The recommended diagnostic test is PCR for mpox (non-variola) Orthopoxvirus, obtaining 2 swabs from each of 2 to 3 lesions using sterile synthetic swabs (https://www.cdc.gov/poxvirus/monkeypox/clinicians/prep-collection-specimens.html). C

CDC criteria for probable case: No suspicion of other recent Orthopoxvirus exposure (e.g., Vaccinia virus in ACAM2000 vaccination) AND demonstration of the presence of Orthopoxvirus DNA by PCR of a clinical specimen OR Orthopoxvirus using immunohistochemical or electron microscopy testing methods OR Demonstration of detectable levels of anti-Orthopoxvirus IgM antibody during the period of 4 to 56 days after rash onset. (https://www.cdc.gov/poxvirus/monkeypox/clinicians/case-definition.html)

CDC criteria for confirmed case: Demonstration of the presence of mpox virus DNA by PCR testing or next-generation sequencing of a clinical specimen OR isolation of mpox virus in culture from a clinical specimen.

In a series of 181 Spanish patients with mpox, 97% were men and 92% were men who have sex with men. Symptoms included flu-like illness (81%), fever (72%), headache (53%), and sore throat (36%). Approximately half of patients reported that these symptoms preceded onset of the rash.

In a series of 1007 US patients, rash (100%), fever (63%), chills (59%), lymphadenopathy (58%), fatigue or malaise (57%), myalgias (55%), and headache (51%) were the most common symptoms. Rectal pain was present in 22% and blood or pus in the stools for 21%. The rash was present on the genitals (46%), arms (40%), face (38%), legs (37%), perianal region (31%), oral mucosa (25%), on the palms (22%) and on the trunk (22%).

In another series of 528 infections in 16 countries, rash (95%), anogenital lesions (73%) and mucosal lesions (41%) were common. Fever (62%), lethargy (41%), myalgias (31%), and headache (27%) were also common. Most patients had lymphadenopathy.

Myalgias and respiratory symptoms are also reported, including a flu-like prodrome. For patients with a flu-like prodromal illness, the rash typically appears 1 to 4 days later. (https://www.cdc.gov/poxvirus/monkeypox/clinicians/clinical-recognition.html)

The characteristic lesions are firm/rubbery, well circumscribed, and may develop umbilication. Most patients (80%) reported between 3 and 20 lesions; 90% reported pustular lesions, 26% vesicular lesions, and 21% papular lesions. Location of lesions included hands and feet (60%), trunk and extremities (57%), genital (55%), perianal (36%), perioral (28%) and oral ulcer (25%).. See representative images in Figures 1-6.

The usual progression is from initial macules (1-2 days), moving to to raised papules (1-2 days), subsequentlyto vesicles with clear fluid (1-2 days) and finally to pustules (5-7 days) that may become pedunculated. (https://www.cdc.gov/poxvirus/monkeypox/clinicians/clinical-recognition.html)
Inguinal lymphadenopathy was present in 61% and cervical lymphadenopathy in 29%.
Complications include proctitis (25%), tonsillitis (10%), and penile edema (8%).
Purulent or bloody stools, rectal bleeding, and rectal pain are typical of the 2022 outbreak.
The usual duration of illness is 2 to 4 weeks. (https://www.cdc.gov/poxvirus/monkeypox/clinicians/clinical-recognition.html)
The recommended diagnostic test is PCR for mpox (non-variola) orthopoxvirus.

CDC recommends obtaining 2 swabs from each of 2 to 3 lesions using sterile synthetic swabs. It is not necessary to unroof the lesion before swabbing. (https://www.cdc.gov/poxvirus/monkeypox/clinicians/prep-collection-specimens.html)
One study of 528 infected persons found that 29% had a concomitant sexually transmitted infection, so routine testing is advised.

Suspect mpox in a patient with characteristic rash, fever, and flu-like symptoms when the disease is circulating in a population. In the most recent outbreak in 2022, it was most likely in men who have sex with men.
Obtain samples using a sterile synthetic swab from 2 to 3 lesions for PCR analysis.
Evaluate the severity of illness and risk factors for severe illness when assessing the need for tecovirimat.
Care is primarily supportive with most patients experiencing a relatively mild illness. C

The CDC recommends tecovirimat for patients with severe disease requiring hospitalization, young children, immunocompromised patients including those with HIV without viral suppression; women who are pregnant or breastfeeding; and patients with complications such as pneumonia, cellulitis, or severe gastroenteritis. C
Initial RCTs however in a range of patients with mpox have not found a clear benefit to tecovirimat.B

Tecovirimat (TPOXX) was developed to treat smallpox, but it has been shown to be effective in animal studies. It is generally well tolerated without serious side effects. It is available in a 200 mg oral capsule and also for IV administration.
However, a randomized placebo-controlled trial of 597 patients in the Democratic Republic of Congo who had clade I mpox found no reduction in days to lesion resolution with tecovirimat.
A retrospective cohort study during the 2022 outbreak also found that patients with and without HIV disease had similar outcomes when given tecovirimat.

As of 2026, the CDC site still recommends tecovirimat for patients with severe disease requiring hospitalization; young children; immunocompromised patients including HIV without viral suppression; persons who are pregnant or breastfeeding; and patients with complications such as pneumonia, cellulitis, or severe gastroenteritis. However, the drug has not been studied in pregnant or breastfeeding persons.

If considered for patients with severe disease, tecovirimat is dosed at 600 mg three times daily for persons weighing >= 120 kg; 600 mg twice daily for persons weighing 40 to 120 kg; 400 mg twice daily for children 25 to 39.9 kg; and 200 mg twice daily for children weighing 13 to 24.9 kg. The drug is given for 14 days.

Brincidofovir (Tembexa) is approved for treatment of smallpox and has been shown in animal studies to have activity against other Orthopoxviruses. (https://www.cdc.gov/poxvirus/monkeypox/clinicians/treatment.html)
Case reports of using cidofovir in patients with comorbid HIV disease have been published with good reported efficacy. More study is needed.
Supportive care includes adequate hydration and nutrition, and monitoring for complications such as secondary bacterial skin infections.
Most patients have self-limited disease that lasts 2 to 4 weeks. B

Mpox has historically been reported to have a mortality rate of 3% to 6%. However, in the 2022 global outbreak, there have been 5 deaths in 18,000 cases (0.03%). This may be due to it being clade 3, which causes less severe disease, to better disease ascertainment and reporting of mild cases, and to the availability of treatments such as tecovirimat. B
